_analysis.relevance_explanation: This demonstrates how AI agents can autonomously produce high-quality, competitive business documents, signaling potential disruption to professional services markets and reducing barriers to entry for new players.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-powered multi-agent systems could automate document authoring at scale, threatening traditional professional services firms and increasing competition in sectors reliant on formal writing.

items.title: CAS: Conformalized Agentic Search via Adaptive Retrieval and Policy Weighting
items.abstract: Search Agents face a severe reliability crisis during reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning. Heuristic Top-K retrieval often causes critical evidence loss or noise inclusion, while over-confidence induced by progressive RL leads to hallucinated answers and redundant searches. To build highly reliable agents, we introduce Conformal Prediction (CP) and propose Conformalized Agentic Search (CAS). This framework establishes reliability guarantees on both the retrieval and training sides: on the retrieval side, an Adaptive Prediction Set (APS), a specific CP realization, translates statistical coverage into dynamic document truncation to construct prediction sets that are adaptive in size; on the training side, Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI), a dynamic CP algorithm, dynamically constructs prediction sets with controllable coverage to quantify answer confidence, which is then used to penalize low-confidence trajectories within the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective, ensuring the model learns only from reliable ones. Experiments across single-hop and multi-hop QA datasets demonstrate that our framework significantly improves reasoning accuracy while drastically redu

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces Conformalized Agentic Search (CAS), a framework using Conformal Prediction (CP) to improve the reliability of AI search agents during reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning. It addresses issues like evidence loss and hallucinated answers by providing statistical guarantees for both retrieval and training, aiming to reduce errors in AI-driven search systems.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: AI search agents with improved reliability could disrupt dominant search platforms by enabling more accurate and trustworthy alternatives, challenging market leaders like Google.
_analysis.market_signal: Reliable AI search agents may accelerate competition in search markets by reducing reliance on traditional search engines, potentially weakening gatekeepers' dominance.

items.title: CARD: Diagnosing Belief to Action Routing Failures in Vision Language Models
items.abstract: Linear probes and activation steering have uncovered that vision-language models (VLMs) internally represent mental states such as agents' beliefs, knowledge, and intentions. However, it is unclear whether and how these representations are used by downstream predictions along these axes. To close this gap, we introduce Cross-Axis Routing Diagnostic (CARD), which steers activations along one axis while measuring the response of a different axis's prediction. Applied to open-weight VLMs on Relay Chain -- a new cooperative grid-world benchmark we propose -- we diagnose a critical routing failure: models fail to incorporate belief representations into their next action prediction, effectively leaving valuable information about their partners unused.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces CARD (Cross-Axis Routing Diagnostic), a tool to test whether vision-language models (VLMs) use their internal representations of mental states (like beliefs or intentions) to make downstream decisions. Using a new benchmark called Relay Chain, the authors find that VLMs often fail to correctly route these internal representations to their final predictions, leading to errors in decision-making.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper reveals a critical failure in how AI models process and act on internal representations, which could impact the reliability and competitiveness of AI-driven systems in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: AI models' routing failures may create opportunities for competitors to develop more reliable alternatives, potentially disrupting dominant AI-powered services.

items.title: Vis-Poison: Poisoning Visual Knowledge in Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.abstract: While multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems increasingly rely on images as external knowledge sources, the introduction of poisoned visual evidence can severely compromise multimodal large language model (MLLM) generation. Unlike prior attacks that rely on altering textual metadata, we introduce Vis-Poison, a novel visual knowledge poisoning attack where the poisoned image itself is the attacker-controlled payload, without manipulating captions, summaries, metadata, or other associated text. Specifically, this attack is instantiated through an automated multi-agent method that constructs visually plausible poisoned images. To assess its impact, we evaluate Vis-Poison across two representative multimodal RAG pipelines, four embedding models, and six generation models. Empirically, Vis-Poison achieves an end-to-end attack success rate of 40.16\% to 65.40\% against 30k-entry multimodal knowledge bases in \emph{black-box} settings. Moreover, Vis-Poison remains effective against various MLLMs that can answer correctly from parametric knowledge alone, with an average success rate above 60\%. Code and data are available at https://github.com/SWUFE-DB-Group/Vis-Poison.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces Vis-Poison, a new type of attack where malicious images are used to trick multimodal AI systems (like those combining images and text) into giving incorrect answers. Unlike previous attacks that alter text, this method directly poisons the visual data these systems rely on, which could lead to harmful outputs without any text manipulation.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper reveals a critical vulnerability in multimodal AI systems that could undermine trust in AI-generated content, potentially affecting competition in AI-driven markets where such systems are gatekeepers or key inputs.
_analysis.market_signal: The rise of adversarial attacks on AI systems signals a need for robust security and reliability standards in AI-driven markets, which could become a competitive differentiator for AI providers.

items.title: Natural-Language-Guided Generator-Agnostic Shortlisting for Protein Binder Design
items.abstract: Modern de novo design workflows generate many candidate protein binders, but wet-lab validation capacity remains limited, making shortlisting a major bottleneck. We study whether LLMs can generate multi-metric ranking policies from precomputed structural-confidence and interface-quality proxy scores. Rather than proposing a new protein binder design pipeline, we focus on post-generation binder shortlisting: selecting the final top-K candidates from already generated binder pools using a shared panel of precomputed proxy scores. On the 10-target held-out split, averaging performance over five sampled global iterative gpt-4o policies reaches 0.589 Recall@10, modestly improving over the strongest single-feature fixed baseline, Protenix binder ipTM, which reaches 0.571 Recall@10. On the 3-target held-out subset comprising Nipah, RBX1, and TREM2, target-conditioned iterative gpt-5.4 policies reach the strongest LLM performance, with 0.519 Recall@10 and 0.583 NDCG@10. These results suggest that LLM-generated ranking policies can act as an interpretable post-generation decision layer for combining heterogeneous proxy metrics to prioritize binders from large candidate pools.

_analysis.summary: This paper explores whether large language models (LLMs) can help select the best protein binders from a large pool of candidates by ranking them based on precomputed structural and interface-quality scores. Instead of designing new proteins, the focus is on improving the shortlisting process using AI-driven ranking policies.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While this paper is about protein design, it highlights how AI-driven ranking systems can optimize selection processes, which may have implications for digital markets where ranking algorithms influence competition.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-powered ranking systems could disrupt traditional selection and recommendation mechanisms in digital markets, potentially altering competitive dynamics.

items.title: Is Multimodal Speculative Decoding Ready for Diffusion-Based Parallel Drafting? A Survey and Empirical Diagnosis
items.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by allowing a lightweight drafter to propose future tokens while a target model verifies them in parallel. Its lossless guarantee has motivated a line of work that pushes the drafter itself toward parallel generation. The most recent paradigm is block-parallel generative drafting, including diffusion-based methods such as DFlash and DSpark, achieving up to 3.6x speedup on common daily chatting tasks. While this transition is well studied in text-only LLMs, its applicability to multimodal models remains an open question. Existing multimodal speculative decoding efforts focus on input compression, adapter alignment, candidate coverage, or modality-specific verification; however, block-parallel generative drafting remains largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, this paper combines a modality-centered survey with a cross-architecture empirical study to ask: Is multimodal speculative decoding ready for diffusion-based parallel drafting? In this survey, we systematically analyze a wide spectrum of multimodal models, spanning Vision-Language, Video-Language, Audio, and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures, from the dual pers

_analysis.summary: This paper examines *speculative decoding*, a technique that speeds up AI text generation by having a smaller 'drafter' model predict future tokens while a larger 'target' model verifies them in parallel. Recent advances like *block-parallel generative drafting* (including diffusion-based methods like DFlash and DSpark) achieve up to 3.6x faster performance in text-only models, but their use in *multimodal models* (AI systems handling text, images, etc.) remains unexplored. The authors call for further research to assess whether these methods can be applied to multimodal AI.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This technology could disrupt the competitive dynamics of AI model providers by reducing the computational costs of large multimodal models, potentially lowering barriers to entry for smaller firms and challenging incumbents like Google, Microsoft, or Meta.
_analysis.market_signal: Faster, cheaper multimodal AI generation could intensify competition in AI services, enabling new entrants to challenge established players in cloud computing, AI-as-a-service, and consumer applications.

items.title: Calibrating Criterion Revision in LLM Agents: Failure Modes and a Trace-Anchored Protocol
items.abstract: Language-model agents can improve after failure or carry text across episodes without revising what counts as success. We study the narrower attribution problem of criterion revision: when criterion K0 accepts an outcome violating a broader commitment B, what observations justify saying that the system formed and persistently used K1? We require five non-compensatory conditions: criterion-failure detection, a model-emitted proposal, new-episode transfer, intervention sensitivity on the claimed carrier, and preservation. We evaluate CMB-0.1 on twelve cross-domain cases and four arms: stateless inference, append-only history, model-generated but harness-committed state, and evaluator-written oracle state. Seven mechanism fixtures yield 84 deterministic scorer trials; four local quantized artifacts yield 96 calls and 192 model-case-arm trials. No model trial satisfies all five conditions, but this zero does not establish general capability absence. Eleven calls remain invalid after one retry; several commitments disclose the target distinction; the harness performs commits; deletion reuses a stateless call; and conflict changes multiple factors. Qwen2.5-7B answers every transfer and p

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how AI agents using large language models (LLMs) can revise their own criteria for success when they fail to meet broader commitments. It identifies five conditions that must be met to confirm that an AI agent has genuinely updated its internal rules (e.g., 'criterion-failure detection' and 'new-episode transfer'). The study evaluates a model called CMB-0.1 across twelve diverse cases to test these conditions.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work highlights how AI agents can autonomously adapt their behavior, which could undermine regulatory frameworks (like the EU's Digital Markets Act) that rely on predictable, rule-bound behavior from dominant platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents capable of self-revising criteria may enable new forms of competitive behavior that bypass existing regulatory oversight, potentially disrupting market structures dominated by large tech platforms.

items.title: DirEAG: Dirichlet Evidence Aggregation for Calibrating Verbalized Confidence in Mathematical Reasoning
items.abstract: Reliable confidence estimation is essential for using large language models in mathematical reasoning, but black-box verbalized confidence is difficult to calibrate. When the same problem is queried under multiple confidence-steering prompts, the resulting answer-confidence observations contain useful uncertainty information, yet their scales may shift across steering levels, models, and datasets. Existing black-box uncertainty methods often rely on answer agreement, sample consistency, or entropy, which describe output variation but do not model the numerical meaning of self-reported confidence. Conversely, direct averaging or heuristic aggregation of elicited confidence cannot learn prompt- and task-dependent bias. We propose DirEAG, a Dirichlet Evidence Aggregation method that converts each elicited answer-confidence observation into calibrated soft evidence over generated candidate answers and an additional null state, allowing the model to represent cases where none of the candidates is correct. Experiments on GSM8K, SVAMP, and GSM-Hard with Qwen, Mistral, and Gemma models show that, compared with direct confidence averaging and heuristic confidence-steering aggregation, DirEA

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces DirEAG, a method to improve how large language models (LLMs) estimate and communicate their confidence in mathematical reasoning tasks. The technique uses multiple confidence-steering prompts to aggregate verbalized confidence scores (self-reported certainty from the model) and calibrate them, addressing inconsistencies in how models report their own reliability.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, the paper highlights the growing role of LLMs in high-stakes decision-making, which could influence market power in AI-driven services and data aggregation.
_analysis.market_signal: Advances in LLM confidence calibration may accelerate the adoption of AI in critical sectors, potentially reinforcing the dominance of firms with superior AI capabilities.

items.title: Towards Faithful Simulation of Human Shopping Behavior
items.abstract: Simulating realistic user shopping behavior underpins offline evaluation and reinforcement learning in e-commerce scenarios. While recent LLM- and VLM-based simulators have made encouraging progress, reproducing a real browsing session remains difficult for two reasons. (i) Memory Challenge: a shopping session spans dozens of pages, yet existing agents either discard long-range observation histories, losing the evolving user state, or naively concatenate them, overwhelming the context window and even degrading simulation quality. (ii) Optimization Challenge: current user simulators are typically supervised to match each logged action via imitation or step-level rewards; the resulting sessions often display unrealistic patterns, such as over-exploration or excessive passivity, which per-step supervision can neither detect nor correct. To address the above challenges, we present RecVerse, a GUI-grounded simulation agent that perceives pages through screenshots and produces faithful multi-turn trajectories. For the memory challenge, RecVerse adopts a cognitive-inspired hierarchical memory: Working Memory for short-term focus, Episodic Memory for in-session traces, and Preference Memor

_analysis.summary: This paper explores how to create realistic AI simulations of human shopping behavior for e-commerce platforms, highlighting two major challenges: (1) managing long-term memory across dozens of browsing pages without losing user context, and (2) optimizing simulations to avoid overwhelming AI models with excessive data. The work focuses on improving 'user simulators'—AI agents designed to mimic real shoppers—which are critical for testing recommendation systems and reinforcement learning in online retail.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This research signals how AI-driven shopping simulators could disrupt e-commerce markets by enabling more sophisticated and adaptive recommendation systems, potentially altering competitive dynamics between platforms and sellers.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-powered shopping simulators may reduce barriers to entry for new e-commerce platforms by improving their ability to personalize and optimize user experiences, intensifying competition with incumbents like Amazon.

items.title: Identity-Aware Human-Object Interaction Motion Captioning
items.abstract: Existing human-object interaction (HOI) motion captioning methods typically describe what happens while referring to the subject using generic terms such as "a person" or "someone", without grounding the caption in subject identity. To address this limitation, we introduce Identity-Aware Human-Object Interaction Motion Captioning task. This task requires each generated caption to specify both the subject identity and the corresponding HOI motion. For example, the model generates "Sub_ID lifts the chair" rather than "A person lifts the chair". For this task, we design identity-aware HOI motion captions based on the BEHAVE and InterCap datasets. We further propose ID-HOINet, which learns from multi-view videos while supporting single-view identity-aware HOI motion caption generation. ID-HOINet contains two core components: Multi-View Identity-Motion Learning Module (MVIML) and Two-Stage Caption Rewriting Strategy (TSCR). MVIML learns from multi-view videos by modeling dependencies across temporal stages and camera viewpoints, capturing identity and interaction motion features. At inference, the TSCR first retrieves the subject identity and generates identity-agnostic HOI motion capti

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces a new task called Identity-Aware Human-Object Interaction (HOI) Motion Captioning, which requires AI models to generate captions that specify both the identity of the subject (e.g., 'Sub_ID' or a named person) and their interaction with an object (e.g., 'lifts the chair'). Current methods typically use generic terms like 'a person,' which lacks specificity. The goal is to improve the precision of AI-generated descriptions by grounding them in identifiable subjects.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While this paper focuses on AI captioning improvements, it signals advancements in AI personalization and identity recognition that could impact digital markets where user-specific data and identity-driven services are central to competition.
_analysis.market_signal: Advances in identity-aware AI captioning may enable more personalized digital services, potentially strengthening platforms that control user identity data.

items.title: VortexChat: An agentic framework for autonomous multi-objective integrated photonic design
items.abstract: The advancement of modern integrated photonics is frequently bottlenecked by device design workflows that rely heavily on manual simulation and expert intuition. While inverse design offers an alternative, it remains constrained by expert supervision and a lack of end-to-end automation. To address these issues, we present VortexChat, an agentic framework for the autonomous, end-to-end inverse design of integrated photonic devices directly from natural language specifications. VortexChat couples a large language model (LLM) decision agent with topology generation, gradient-based refinement, and full-wave electromagnetic simulation. This closed-loop architecture enables the system to iteratively decompose design objectives, orchestrate computational tools, and update strategies based on feedback with minimal human intervention. Constrained by the absolute metrics of the Vortex100 Benchmark, VortexChat autonomously generates devices that strictly meet all predefined performance thresholds without any human-in-the-loop. As an experimental demonstration, we fabricated a broadband terahertz perfect vortex beam multiplexer, autonomously designed by VortexChat, with measurements confirming

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces VortexChat, an AI-powered system that automates the design of integrated photonic devices (tiny chips that manipulate light) using natural language instructions. It replaces manual, expert-driven workflows with an autonomous 'agentic framework' combining large language models (LLMs) with optimization tools, reducing reliance on human supervision.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about digital markets, the paper demonstrates how AI-driven automation in specialized hardware design could disrupt traditional industry structures, potentially affecting competition in niche tech sectors.
_analysis.market_signal: Autonomous AI agents in technical design workflows may accelerate innovation cycles, challenging incumbent firms in specialized hardware markets.

items.title: CDRL: Certification-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Neutrino Flavor Model Discovery
items.abstract: Many scientific discovery problems require searching combinatorial hypothesis spaces under complex domain constraints. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach, but existing methods rely on scalar rewards that provide limited information about why candidate solutions fail, leading agents to repeatedly explore invalid regions. We introduce Certification-Driven Reinforcement Learning (CDRL), a framework that leverages structured feedback from symbolic reasoning tools. When a candidate violates domain constraints, these tools produce certificates identifying the actions responsible for failure. CDRL converts these certificates into reusable constraints that eliminate classes of invalid solutions and guide exploration toward valid regions. We evaluate CDRL on neutrino flavor model discovery in theoretical particle physics, where the hypothesis space exceeds $10^{26}$ possible models, and compare it with the state-of-the-art RL approach previously used for this task. Across three theory spaces, CDRL achieves up to 1.95$\times$ higher valid model rates and up to 6.33$\times$ higher neutrino model rates while evaluating up to 4$\times$ fewer candidates. We further extract 4

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces Certification-Driven Reinforcement Learning (CDRL), a new method for solving complex scientific problems by using reinforcement learning (RL) agents guided by structured feedback from symbolic reasoning tools. When an agent’s candidate solution violates domain constraints, these tools provide 'certificates'—detailed explanations pinpointing which actions caused the failure—helping the agent avoid invalid regions more efficiently.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While CDRL improves RL efficiency in constrained environments, it does not directly address digital competition policy but signals potential for AI systems to handle complex, rule-bound tasks in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: AI systems capable of generating structured, interpretable feedback (like CDRL) could enable more autonomous and compliant digital platforms, reducing regulatory oversight burdens.

items.title: Temporal Validity on Real Software Histories: Eliminating Stale-Fact Errors in Code-Assistant Memory over GitHub Fixes
items.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has no model of time: when a fact changes across a coding session - a function is renamed, an endpoint moves, a dependency is bumped - RAG retrieves both the old and new value with near-identical similarity and cannot tell which is current, so it serves the superseded value. Paper 1 showed, on synthetic single-value benchmarks, that a deterministic (subject, relation, object) supersession memory eliminates this failure. Here we validate it end-to-end on real software history. From 707 real GitHub issues (SWE-bench Lite + Verified) we extract 130 clean atomic state transitions, a fix that changes one identifiable value from a pre-fix to a post-fix form, and render each marker-free (the stale and current statements differ only in the value). On this set, MemStrata reaches 0.91 answer accuracy versus RAG's 0.57-0.59; and, the structural result, when forced to answer RAG serves the superseded value 36-38% of the time (an LLM reranker does not help) while MemStrata drives this to ~0, at RAG retrieval latency (~2.1 s vs ~18 s for the reranker). We are explicit about scope: only ~18% of real fixes are clean atomic transitions; Paper 2 isolates the memo

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how AI coding assistants (like GitHub Copilot) can make mistakes by relying on outdated code information when software evolves over time. It tests a solution called 'supersession memory' on real GitHub issues to ensure AI tools use current facts, reducing errors in software development.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Highlights how AI tools' reliance on outdated data could create inefficiencies in software markets, indirectly affecting competition among developers and platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-powered coding assistants may become critical infrastructure in software development, potentially centralizing control over developer workflows.

items.title: Why2Speak: Faithful Reasoning for Abstaining Action Policies
items.abstract: Many agentic systems must repeatedly choose between acting and abstaining, making faithful reasoning important for oversight: an explanation is useful only if it reflects the computation that produced the action. We study this problem through intervention timing in multi-party conversation, where an assistant must decide whether to speak or remain silent. This setting exposes class imbalance, asymmetric action costs, and the possibility that exposing reasoning changes the policy being audited. Using Qwen3-8B, decoded with or without chain-of-thought reasoning, we compare direct decision policies, reasoning policies, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. We find a capability-auditability tradeoff: the strongest direct policy achieves higher quality but exposes no reasoning to inspect, while the reasoning policy provides a trace at the cost of lower performance, particularly recall of true intervention opportunities. Supervised fine-tuning either suppresses reasoning or preserves it without improving decision quality, while reinforcement learning also fails to improve the reasoning policy. We identify one mechanism underlying this failure: group relative objectives prov

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how AI agents (like chatbots) decide when to 'speak' (take action) or 'abstain' (remain silent) in conversations, focusing on the importance of transparent reasoning for oversight. It tests whether showing an AI’s step-by-step thought process (chain-of-thought reasoning) improves its decision-making compared to direct responses, using the Qwen3-8B model.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The paper highlights how AI decision-making transparency (or lack thereof) can impact oversight and trust in automated systems, which is critical for regulating AI-driven platforms and ensuring fair competition.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents with faithful reasoning could disrupt markets by enabling more reliable and auditable automated decision-making, potentially reducing reliance on opaque proprietary systems.

items.title: Amplifying the imaging power of digital sky surveys with space telescopes data and generative AI
items.abstract: While Digital sky surveys provide excellent throughput of image data and can cover a large footprint, their imaging power is normally inferior to that of space-based telescopes. Space-based telescopes, on the other hand, provide excellent imaging power and can image the deep Universe, but cannot provide the same throughput as advanced ground-based sky surveys. Here, we utilize generative AI to elevate the quality of galaxy images taken by ground-based telescopes to the level of details enabled by space telescopes. The solution is based on the nature of galaxy shapes, allowing generative AI trained on space-based images to convert weak signal into detailed and clear galaxy images. The method allows for combining the high throughput of ground-based sky surveys with the image quality of space-based telescopes. The source code for the method is available, as well as paired training data and a catalog of 63,202 galaxy images enhanced by the proposed method. We also provide a software tool that encapsulates the entire pipeline and the custom generative AI model to generate galaxy images with enhanced quality.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper explores how generative AI can enhance the quality of galaxy images captured by ground-based digital sky surveys to match the detail provided by space-based telescopes. The authors leverage the inherent properties of galaxy shapes to train AI models that improve imaging resolution, effectively bridging the gap between ground and space telescope capabilities.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on astronomical imaging, it highlights the growing role of generative AI in improving data quality from lower-cost sources, which could have indirect implications for digital markets where data quality and access drive competitive advantages.
_analysis.market_signal: Generative AI's ability to enhance lower-quality data sources may reduce reliance on high-cost, high-precision data providers, signaling potential shifts in data market dynamics.

items.title: DreamBench-SWE: A Multi-Session Memory-Hygiene Benchmark for Software Agents
items.abstract: DreamBench-SWE is a multi-session benchmark for software-agent memory hygiene in which later software tasks depend on non-inferable evidence from earlier sessions and are scored by executable hidden oracles. We report the original scaled v2 fold and a separately preregistered v2.1 successor audit designed after that study but frozen before successor outcome inspection. The successor run completed 360/360 work units and 720/720 S3 cells across four conditions. In the original fold, the primary DF-hybrid--B5 contrast was null (95/180 versus 89/180; clustered p=.518, Holm p=1), not evidence of equivalence, and C9/C10 retained B0-headroom limitations. In the successor, no external memory achieved 21/180 passes (rate 0.1167), deterministic verbatim event memory 82/180 (rate 0.4556), the typed-plus-raw reference probe 83/180 (rate 0.4611), and one pinned hosted Mem0 literal-storage configuration 97/180 (rate 0.5389). The registered six-slot Family A retained unavailable slots at p=1; all three available comparisons against no memory rejected after Holm correction. Both preregistered mechanism contrasts were unavailable after pre-evaluation conformance rejection. The secondary literal-sto

_analysis.summary: DreamBench-SWE is a benchmark designed to test the memory hygiene of AI software agents, meaning their ability to retain and use information from past sessions when performing new tasks. The study found no significant difference between two AI models (DF-hybrid and B5) in their ability to handle multi-session tasks that depend on earlier evidence.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper signals how AI agents may evolve to handle complex, multi-session tasks, which could impact market competition in sectors reliant on AI-driven workflows.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents with improved memory hygiene could disrupt markets where task continuity and data retention are critical, such as software development or customer service automation.

items.title: Auditable by Construction: An Ontology-Driven Framework for Trustworthy LLM Analytics in Enterprise Finance
items.abstract: Enterprise adoption of large language models in finance is constrained less by fluency than by trust: in Financial Planning and Analysis (FP&A) and other regulated workflows, an answer is usable only if it is traceable to authoritative sources and auditable after the fact. This paper argues that retrieval-augmented generation for enterprise finance should be evaluated on auditability alongside accuracy, and presents the Knowledge-Driven Analytics Framework (KDAF), which builds ontology-driven knowledge systems through six iterative stages and retrieves evidence via Context-Aware Relevance Propagation (CARP), so that every retrieved fact carries its relationship type, confidence, and source lineage. An evaluation on FinanceBench (145 questions) compares KDAF against zero-context inference, BM25, concept-weighted lexical retrieval, and ungrounded graph traversal. First, retrieval is necessary: zero-context inference reaches 4.1% correctness against 10-12% for retrieval-augmented conditions. Second, on answer correctness the retrieval conditions are statistically indistinguishable (KDAF vs BM25: -0.007, 95% CI [-0.021, 0.000]), so accuracy alone does not justify structured retrieval h

_analysis.summary: This paper argues that large language models (LLMs) used in enterprise finance need to be auditable—meaning their answers must be traceable to trusted sources—to gain trust in regulated workflows like financial planning. It proposes the Knowledge-Driven Analytics Framework (KDAF), which uses ontology-driven knowledge systems and retrieval-augmented generation to ensure answers are evidence-based and verifiable.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, the paper highlights how auditability and traceability in AI systems could reshape trust in digital markets, particularly for regulated sectors like finance.
_analysis.market_signal: The framework signals a growing demand for transparent, auditable AI systems in high-stakes industries, which may influence how regulators and firms approach accountability in digital markets.

items.title: Beyond Effectiveness: A Multi-Criteria Framework for Comparing Practical Socio-Technical Interventions
items.abstract: Designers and policymakers in sociotechnical domains like content moderation, privacy interfaces, recommender systems and beyond, must choose among a growing menu of proposed interventions, but typically lack a principled basis for comparing them. Prior work tends to evaluate interventions individually and mostly along the effectiveness criteria, while implementation constraints such as cost, effort and feasibility are often considered separately. We present a multi-criteria framework for evaluating sociotechnical interventions. This framework is instantiated through the case of misinformation, a domain of intense focus for proposed countermeasures. We survey $N=39$ researchers on 40 operationalized interventions across five evaluative criteria: political feasibility, effectiveness, user acceptance, cost, and implementation effort. We find that the interventions that experts judge to be the most effective are not always the most acceptable to the public or the most feasible to implement. We also discuss how this tension has implications for the design of sociotechnical interventions beyond misinformation, and offer a decision framework for practitioners navigating the trade-offs of

_analysis.summary: This academic paper proposes a multi-criteria framework for evaluating sociotechnical interventions (like content moderation or recommender systems) beyond just effectiveness. It argues that policymakers and designers need a more comprehensive way to compare interventions, considering factors like cost, effort, and feasibility alongside performance. The framework is demonstrated through the case of misinformation.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, the paper's focus on evaluating interventions in digital platforms (e.g., recommender systems) provides methodological insights relevant to assessing platform obligations under laws like the DMA (the EU's Digital Markets Act).
_analysis.market_signal: Signals a shift toward more holistic, evidence-based policymaking for digital platform interventions, which could influence future regulatory design.

items.title: One Hierarchy, Two Systems: Semantic Product IDs for Discovery-Surface Ranking and Search-Page Query Reformulation
items.abstract: Multi-merchant e-commerce catalogs contain equivalent and related products under different merchant-scoped identifiers, fragmenting behavioral evidence across merchants. Expert-defined taxonomies, meanwhile, are often too coarse for fine-grained discovery. We investigate whether a single hierarchical Semantic ID (\sid{}) representation can support personalized ranking and query reformulation. Learned once from product-content embeddings, the hierarchy defines product concepts at multiple granularities that each application combines with its own behavioral and serving context. For ranking, we aggregate consumer affinity and product performance over \sid{} prefixes and derive sequence features for candidate products and consumer histories. Controlled ablations show improved offline relevance, while online evaluation of the full ranking treatment shows stronger top-slot add-to-cart engagement and broader exposure for less-popular products. For query reformulation, we ground queries and session transitions in \sid{} concepts, use the hierarchy for navigation and refinement, and filter suggestions against the merchant's assortment. Offline evaluation shows finer intent preservation than

_analysis.summary: This paper explores whether a single hierarchical system of Semantic Product IDs (SIDs) can improve how products are ranked and searched in multi-merchant e-commerce platforms. The authors argue that traditional taxonomies are too broad, while merchant-specific identifiers fragment data, and propose a unified approach to better personalize rankings and query reformulations.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work signals how AI-driven product categorization and ranking systems could reshape competitive dynamics in e-commerce markets by enabling more precise discovery and reducing reliance on dominant platforms' proprietary algorithms.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-powered semantic product identification may reduce barriers to entry for smaller e-commerce platforms by improving discovery without relying on gatekeeper-controlled taxonomies.

items.title: ARQ: Agentic CodeQL Query Refinement for C/C++ Vulnerability Detection
items.abstract: Static analyzers have been widely adopted for vulnerability detection in C/C++ programs. Query-based static analyzers (e.g., CodeQL) encode vulnerable code patterns in detection queries and match them against source code. However, existing queries still suffer from false positives (FPs, incorrectly flagging benign code as vulnerable) and false negatives (FNs, missing real vulnerabilities). We present ARQ, an agentic framework that automatically refines C/C++ CodeQL queries using execution-grounded evidence from synthesized C/C++ programs. Our key insight is that a synthesized program exposes a query's weakness whenever its execution disagrees with the query's verdict. If the program is genuinely vulnerable but the query stays silent, the query has an FN weakness; if the program is safe but the query fires anyway, it has an FP weakness. ARQ then runs an LLM-based refinement loop that repairs the query using these disagreements as ground truth. Unlike previous query refining methods, ARQ requires no labeled datasets, no commit history, and no vulnerability-specific templates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ARQ by refining 12 official CodeQL queries using three commercial LLMs (G

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces ARQ, an AI-powered system that automatically improves the accuracy of CodeQL queries, which are used to detect security vulnerabilities in C/C++ software. By generating and testing synthetic programs, ARQ reduces false positives (incorrectly flagging safe code as vulnerable) and false negatives (missing real vulnerabilities) in static code analysis.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about digital competition, the paper highlights the growing role of AI agents in automating complex tasks like software security, which could influence market dynamics in developer tools and cybersecurity.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-driven automation in software security may reduce barriers to entry for new cybersecurity firms, challenging incumbents like GitHub Advanced Security or Snyk.

items.title: AgentMercury: Your Agent Can Synthesize Verifiable Environments for Business Scenarios at scale
items.abstract: Agents learn to act through interaction with environments, yet the environments used for training are often manually constructed or synthesized around predefined tasks and benchmarks. This task-centric paradigm makes it difficult to scale environments that reflect realistic and evolving workflows where diverse tasks can naturally emerge from the underlying world. We introduce AgentMercury, a scalable framework for synthesizing executable environments from high-level business scenarios. Rather than constructing an environment for a specific task, AgentMercury first instantiates a persistent world with entities, services, tools, state, and executable cross-service invariants, from which diverse tasks and interaction trajectories can subsequently emerge. We construct 4,783 executable environments spanning 14 industries and 50 countries, and use them as training substrates for reinforcement learning. Despite being generated without targeting the evaluation benchmarks, policies trained on these business-oriented environments improve substantially on both enterprise workflows and out-of-domain benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, scientific computing, and tool use. In our experiments,

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces AgentMercury, a framework that uses AI agents to automatically create and simulate realistic business environments from high-level scenarios, rather than relying on static, task-specific benchmarks. By enabling scalable, dynamic environment generation, it could accelerate the development of AI systems that interact with complex, evolving workflows in real-world markets.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: AgentMercury’s ability to generate realistic, scalable business environments signals a shift toward AI systems that can autonomously navigate and compete in digital markets, potentially reducing barriers to entry for new players and challenging incumbents' control over data and workflows.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-driven environment synthesis could democratize access to realistic market simulations, enabling smaller firms to develop and test AI-driven business models without relying on incumbents' proprietary data or platforms.

items.title: Weighted Memory Tree: Remembering What Matters for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated the ability to solve multi-step tasks requiring planning, tool use, and external information access, yet growing execution histories increase inference cost and expose reasoning to outdated, irrelevant, or misleading information, potentially degrading reasoning quality. Existing memory approaches organize or compress execution histories but provide limited mechanisms for deciding which memories remain active. We introduce the, a hierarchical memory system that organizes execution into tasks, subtasks, and actions while assigning each memory a dynamic retention score. Event-based updates and selection-based decay revise these scores, allowing WMT to preserve useful information, fold completed trajectories, suppress low-utility content, and retain access to folded context. We evaluate WMT on GAIA-Text using Qwen3-8B, Gemma 4 E4B, and Llama-3.1-8B, with ablations and memory-poisoning experiments. Relative to linear memory, WMT improves accuracy by an average of 9.97 percentage points while reducing prompt-token usage by 32.8%. Memory-poisoning experiments show that WMT limits the persistence and propagation of unreliable information.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces a new memory system for AI agents called the Weighted Memory Tree, which helps them remember only the most important information from long tasks to avoid confusion from outdated or irrelevant data. By organizing memories hierarchically (tasks, subtasks, actions) and weighting their importance, the system improves efficiency and reasoning quality in multi-step AI workflows.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper signals a shift toward more efficient and autonomous AI agents, which could reduce reliance on dominant platforms (e.g., search engines or app stores) by enabling AI to perform complex tasks independently.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents with advanced memory systems may disrupt platform dependency by performing tasks end-to-end, challenging gatekeepers' control over user workflows.

items.title: Characterizations of continuous adequate objective functions for ordinal or interval scaled data
items.abstract: Objective functions (goodness criteria which have to be optimized) that are considered, for instance, in cluster analysis, factor analysis, (linear) structural equation modeling, (linear) regression, multidimensional scaling, choice theory, and utility theory, must be {\em adequate}, i.e. carefully adapted to the structure of the observed data. Adequateness of an objective function means, in our terminology, that (certain) transformations of its arguments, e.g. changes in the unit measures of the quantities involved, do not influence the solutions of the optimization procedure. In this paper we concentrate our attention on affine strictly increasing transformations and we also incorporate the case of continuous adequate objective functions accordingly. The characterization of adequate dissimilarity coefficients for interval scaled data shows the appropriateness of the concept of adequateness that is developed in this paper.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper discusses how to design objective functions (criteria for optimization) that are 'adequate' for different types of data scales, such as ordinal or interval data. Adequateness here means that the optimization solutions remain consistent even if the units of measurement change. The paper explores how transformations of data inputs should not affect the outcomes of optimization procedures like cluster analysis or regression.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper is highly technical and focuses on mathematical optimization, it indirectly relates to digital competition policy by highlighting the importance of data quality and measurement in algorithmic decision-making, which is central to many digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: This work signals the growing need for robust and consistent data handling in digital markets, where algorithmic systems rely heavily on optimization functions.

items.title: The Order of Binary Experiments under Endogenous Stopping
items.abstract: We study the comparison of binary statistical experiments in large samples where information is acquired sequentially and the number of observations can depend on realized evidence. We introduce two orders. Stopping dominance compares experiments by their ability to reproduce the outcomes of arbitrary stopping policies, while decision dominance compares their value in finite decision problems with costly observations. Our main result shows that the two orders coincide and are characterized by coordinatewise dominance of the two directed Kullback--Leibler divergences. Moreover, strict dominance implies eventual strict value dominance in every decision problem in which learning the state can change the optimal action. The key result behind this characterization is an exact simulation theorem: any binary target experiment can be generated from repeated observations of a source experiment with expected sample sizes attaining the two KL lower bounds up to an additive constant that depends only on the source.

_analysis.summary: This paper studies how to compare statistical experiments where data is gathered sequentially and stopping rules can depend on early results. It introduces two new ways to rank these experiments: *stopping dominance* (how well an experiment can mimic other stopping rules) and *decision dominance* (how useful it is in decision-making with costly observations). The authors prove these two rankings are the same and are determined by comparing two measures called *directed Kullback-Leibler divergences* (measures of information loss between probability distributions).
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on statistical theory, its insights into sequential data collection and stopping rules could indirectly inform how digital platforms optimize data-driven strategies, potentially affecting market dynamics.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals growing academic interest in sequential decision-making in data-rich environments, which may influence how platforms design algorithms and data collection strategies.

items.title: Random Cap: Optimal Informationally Robust Delegation
items.abstract: Are simple delegation rules optimal under ambiguity? We study delegation when the principal knows the mean, but not the distribution, of the agent's private information. In a quadratic constant-bias environment, the robustly optimal randomized mechanism is a random cap: the principal draws and reveals an upper bound below which the agent chooses freely. Randomization strictly outperforms every deterministic cap by hedging against cap-specific worst-case distributions. We characterize random caps through nondecreasing and concave expected-action rules and construct the solution using a saddle-point approach. The worst-case distribution features an exponential survival function over its continuous region and an atom at the upper endpoint. Under regularity conditions, the result extends to convex-order ambiguity. When the mean is below the agent's bias, the optimal mechanism additionally requires an incentive-neutral outcome lottery.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines whether simple delegation rules (like fixed limits) are optimal when a decision-maker (the 'principal') has incomplete information about an agent's private data. It finds that a randomized approach—called a 'random cap'—where the principal sets a variable upper limit on the agent's actions, performs better than fixed rules by reducing risks from worst-case scenarios. The solution involves designing non-decreasing and concave expected-action rules to construct this optimal mechanism.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper contributes to platform economics by demonstrating how principals (e.g., regulators or large platforms) can design delegation mechanisms that mitigate risks from asymmetric information, which is central to digital market competition.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals a shift toward more adaptive and robust regulatory or platform governance mechanisms in digital markets, where fixed rules may be suboptimal.

items.title: When Failures Propagate: Causal Failure Attribution in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.abstract: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) interleaves retrieval, reasoning, and answer generation across multiple hops. A retrieval error at hop 1 can surface only as a wrong answer at hop 3, while later retrieval can also repair the trajectory. This paper introduces AgenticRAG-FP, an interventional benchmark for causal failure attribution in agentic RAG. The benchmark injects a certified fault at a specified hop, re-executes the downstream trajectory, and evaluates diagnosers against the known intervention. Its central question is whether a post-hoc trace still identifies the injected hop after the suffix changes. In the completed strict dense Claude Haiku 4.5 sweep on 80 three-hop MuSiQue questions, coverage-based diagnosis is 0.91 at hop 1 and 0.00 at hops 2 and 3 (n=43,36,21 failed trajectories). A smaller content-corruption study changes an answer-bearing or bridge fact in topically intact evidence. At depth 2, where 18 failed cases remain after filtering, coverage-based diagnosis is 0.00 and a frozen-hop counterfactual probe is 0.67 in an exploratory pooled comparison. Depth-3 content estimates are descriptive only because they contain three failed cases. These results mak

_analysis.summary: This paper studies agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), a system where AI agents retrieve information, reason, and generate answers across multiple steps. It introduces AgenticRAG-FP, a benchmark that deliberately injects errors at specific steps to test whether AI systems can correctly identify where failures occur. The study finds that errors in early steps may only appear later, making diagnosis harder.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work reveals how AI systems' internal failure propagation can obscure the true sources of errors, which is critical for assessing liability, accountability, and market power in AI-driven digital services.
_analysis.market_signal: AI systems with opaque failure propagation may challenge regulators' ability to enforce competition rules or hold platforms accountable for harmful outcomes.

items.title: Applying Anthropic Primitives at Large Enterprises: Harness Paradigm for Knowledge Work
items.abstract: Frontier models have collapsed the cost of writing custom code: a niche problem a specialist sees in their own domain now costs an afternoon. The cost of reviewing and maintaining that code hasn't collapsed. Each solution drifts from the next; understanding one means reading its codebase from scratch. Large enterprises build something centrally governed instead: at worst an off-the-shelf product, at best a graph-orchestration framework wired bespoke per use case, or a low-code platform used as the orchestrator. These are custom every time and limited in scope. Enterprises don't weigh a third option that escapes both constraints: the harness paradigm. Recent work treats the coding-agent harness as enterprise infrastructure rather than a coding tool, converging on three findings: harnesses suffice at the task level and outperform more elaborate architectures on enterprise work (arXiv:2604.00073, arXiv:2604.13107); harness choice accounts for most of the variance in agent benchmark results, more than model choice does (arXiv:2605.23950); and the gap between that finding and enterprise adoption is governance (arXiv:2605.10223, arXiv:2605.18747). We propose an architecture that closes t

_analysis.summary: This paper discusses how frontier AI models (like large language models) are making it cheaper and faster to write custom code for niche business problems, but notes that maintaining and scaling these solutions remains costly and fragmented. It argues that large enterprises often resort to centralized, bespoke solutions (e.g., low-code platforms or orchestration frameworks) that are inflexible and limited in scope, highlighting inefficiencies in enterprise AI adoption.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: It reveals structural challenges in enterprise AI adoption that could influence market dynamics for AI tooling providers and large tech platforms offering enterprise solutions.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that the high cost of maintaining AI-generated solutions may create opportunities for specialized enterprise AI platforms or orchestration tools, potentially reshaping competition in the B2B AI market.

items.title: Dual-Cache Latent Space Communication between Heterogeneous Language Models
items.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems split work across models, so answering often requires knowledge that sits in another agent's context: a Sharer has encoded information that a Receiver needs to complete its task. They usually communicate by exchanging text, which puts autoregressive decoding on the critical path and reduces the exchange to a discrete message written without sight of the receiver's state. Recent latent protocols instead translate the sharer's key-value (KV) cache into the receiver's: C2C supports heterogeneous models but requires both to read the same input, while LCF-X removes this shared-context requirement through position-free sharer-cache pooling. Three restrictions remain: LCF-X compresses the sharer alone, supplies the same layer-local summary to every receiver position with no joint cross-layer memory to retrieve from, and assumes matched layer count and KV geometry. We introduce XKV, which lifts all three: learned-query attention pools both caches; self-attention over receiver-aligned layer tokens, with a learned layer map reconciling different depths, mixes the pooled summaries into a compact joint memory; and a shared position decoder lets every raw receiver cache

_analysis.summary: This paper proposes a new way for AI language models (LLMs) to share information more efficiently by exchanging compressed 'latent space' data (key-value caches) instead of text. This avoids delays caused by slow text generation and allows different models to work together even if they process inputs differently.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This technology could reduce barriers to entry for smaller AI model providers by enabling them to collaborate with larger models without relying on text-based APIs, potentially disrupting the dominance of big tech firms in AI services.
_analysis.market_signal: Latent space communication between AI models signals a shift toward more modular and interoperable AI systems, which could erode the control of gatekeeper platforms over AI workflows.

items.title: Evaluating Skills, Not Just Agents: Agentic Continuous Evaluation of Skills
items.abstract: Enterprise agent programs are moving from prototypes into production, where reusable skills, tools, and workflow packages must be reviewed with evidence rather than prose. Current gates often scan these artifacts for structure, style, and security, but they do not answer the deployment question: does the capability package help a live agent complete enterprise tasks under the same model, sandbox, and grading policy? We present ACES (Agentic Continuous Evaluation of Skills), a repository-native framework for evaluating skills and product capability packages as executable agent artifacts. ACES runs paired live trials with and without a target skill, normalizes trajectories into the Agent Trajectory Interchange Format (ATIF), grades six default runtime metrics, and reports Skill Lift: the target skill's added value for a fixed task, harness, workspace, and scorer. The same protocol supports product-owned task suites that compare baseline, skill, bundle, team-skill, and plugin targets. On 145 real skills from internal enterprise repositories and public catalogs, scan-only gates surface useful authoring issues but measure complementary facets (structural versus LLM-judge Spearman $ρ= 0.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces ACES (Agentic Continuous Evaluation of Skills), a new framework for testing AI agents' capabilities by running them in real-world-like environments to see if they can complete tasks effectively. Instead of just checking code structure or security, it evaluates whether reusable AI 'skills' (small, modular AI tools) actually work in practice within enterprise systems.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: ACES signals how AI agent ecosystems could shift competitive dynamics by enabling modular, reusable AI tools that reduce dependency on single providers' proprietary systems.
_analysis.market_signal: The rise of standardized, executable AI skills could lower barriers to entry for competitors in enterprise AI markets, challenging incumbents like Microsoft or Google.

items.title: JuryProbe: An Empirical Consensus-Risk Diagnostic for Routing Reference-Free Factuality Judge Panels to Grounded Verification
items.abstract: Panels of inexpensive LLM judges increasingly make accept-or-escalate decisions. In factuality settings, accepting a claim because several reference-free judges agree can create a hidden risk: agreement may reflect shared false-negative blind spots rather than independent evidence. We introduce JuryProbe, an empirical consensus-risk diagnostic for reference-free factuality judge panels, paired with a calibration-based routing policy. JuryProbe estimates consensus risk from a labeled calibration probe using false-negative-only (FN-only) judge correlation and false-consensus lift; when flagged high-risk, reference-free majority accepts are routed to the same judges with trusted references. On audited FEVER corruptions, reference-free panels show correlated false negatives (FN-only correlations 0.402 and 0.368; lifts 3.13x and 18.13x), while unanimous false consensus drops to zero under a trusted-reference best-case diagnostic on both minimal-pair and non-minimal-pair evidence. In flagged settings, the routed policy is by construction equivalent to grounding every reference-free majority accept (verified in 34/34 splits): improvement comes from accept-conditioned grounding, while the

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces *JuryProbe*, a tool to detect hidden risks in AI judge panels that evaluate factual claims. These panels often rely on multiple AI models ('LLM judges') to agree on whether a claim is true, but their shared blind spots can lead to false consensus. The authors propose a diagnostic to measure this 'consensus risk' and a routing policy to improve reliability.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Highlights systemic risks in AI-driven content moderation and verification systems, which are critical for platform governance and could influence regulatory scrutiny of AI-powered decision-making in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: AI judge systems may become a new layer of infrastructure for content moderation and fact-checking, potentially creating new gatekeepers or dependencies in digital ecosystems.

items.title: Testing and Evaluation of Agentic AI Systems In Military Command and Control
items.abstract: Agentic AI systems are being procured for military command and control (C2) under public commitments to rigorous testing and human oversight. Whether such commitments can be discharged depends on their supporting assurance case, which requires three elements: claims specifying the conditions for acceptability, evidence bearing on those claims, and an argument connecting the two. Through a structured review of 240 documented Testing and Evaluation (T&E) practices, spanning eight evaluation dimensions and three lifecycle stages, we identify eight assumptions that established methods make about their test article, grouped into four clusters: system specifiability, stability, composability, and supervisability. Agentic properties weaken all eight assumptions. This erosion affects the argument connecting evidence to claims, not the claims or evidence themselves. As a result, test results may satisfy process requirements, but they do not warrant the inference from tested to fielded behavior. We derive ten assurance claims for the first three assumption clusters and assess whether current and emerging methods can address each, mapping operational consequences through five C2 scenarios. Su

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how *agentic AI systems* (AI systems that can act autonomously to achieve goals) are being tested for use in military *command and control* (C2) systems, which are systems that help leaders make and execute decisions. It argues that these systems require a strong *assurance case*—a structured argument showing they are safe and reliable—built on clear claims, evidence, and reasoning. The study reviews 240 testing methods across eight evaluation areas and three lifecycle stages, revealing eight key assumptions that current testing approaches rely on.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on military AI testing, its framework for evaluating autonomous systems could inform regulatory approaches to AI safety and accountability in digital markets, particularly for high-risk AI applications.
_analysis.market_signal: This signals growing scrutiny of autonomous AI systems' reliability and oversight, which may influence future digital competition policies focused on AI governance and accountability.

items.title: AgentDecarbonizer: Carbon-Aware Execution for AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents extend large language models from single prompt-response interactions to long-running, goaldirected workflows that issue many model calls, invoke tools, and interact with external environments. These workflows enable tasks such as software repair, data analysis, and experiment management, but their repeated model invocations can incur substantial carbon emissions. This paper characterizes the carbon emissions of OpenClaw agent workloads using WildClawBench, and shows that emissions depend on token consumption, context cache reuse, and the carbon intensity of the grid. Our characterization identifies deadline flexibility as an opportunity for carbon-aware execution: agent tasks can wait for lower-carbon-intensity periods or shift to lower-carbon grids. However, doing so requires handling uncertain execution time for temporal shifting and cached context recomputation during spatial shifting. We present AgentDecarbonizer, a carbon optimizer for AI agents that runs alongside OpenClaw. Given a task prompt and user-specified deadline, AgentDecarbonizer conservatively estimates task duration and selects deadline-feasible execution schedules, while accounting for cache recomputat

_analysis.summary: This paper studies the carbon emissions of AI agents—software systems that use large language models (LLMs) to perform long-running tasks like software repair or data analysis. It finds that emissions depend on how many tokens (words or symbols) the AI processes, how efficiently it reuses cached information, and the carbon intensity of the electricity grid powering the data centers. The authors use OpenClaw agent workloads and WildClawBench to measure these emissions.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, this paper highlights the growing energy demands of AI agents, which could influence market dynamics by increasing costs for smaller firms and reinforcing the dominance of large cloud providers with superior infrastructure.
_analysis.market_signal: The rising energy costs of AI agents may accelerate consolidation in the AI infrastructure market, favoring well-resourced cloud providers and potentially raising barriers to entry for smaller competitors.

items.title: Consilience: Conformally Calibrated Communication Control for Hidden-Profile Multi-Agent Reasoning
items.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems can improve reasoning by pooling diverse perspectives, but their effectiveness depends on coordinating communication, particularly in hidden-profile settings where each agent holds only part of the evidence required for a correct decision. Existing protocols, including fixed schedules, round-robin exchange, and unstructured debate, provide no guarantee that a conversational action is appropriate. We propose Consilience, an inference-time orchestration framework that both steers and certifies multi-agent communication under distributed private information. At each turn, Consilience summarizes the discussion using a compact state capturing uncertainty, disagreement, evidence gain, redundancy, and premature consensus, then selects both a communication intervention (challenge, clarify, seek evidence, or route) and an appropriate speaker. Its central contribution is a round-wise conformal calibration procedure that provides a distribution-free, finite-sample guarantee: at each discussion round, conditional on reaching that round, the one-step regret of a controller's proposed action is bounded by a calibrated threshold with marginal probability at least 1 - alpha

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces *Consilience*, a new framework for coordinating communication among multiple AI agents (large language models or LLMs) to improve decision-making when information is scattered across agents (a 'hidden-profile' setting). The framework uses inference-time rules to steer and validate conversations, ensuring agents share and evaluate evidence effectively without relying on unstructured or inefficient debate methods.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how AI agent coordination could reduce inefficiencies in decentralized decision-making, potentially disrupting markets where centralized control (e.g., by dominant platforms) currently dominates.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals the rise of AI multi-agent systems that could challenge the dominance of single-platform decision-making in sectors like search, recommendation, and enterprise software.

items.title: Beyond End-to-End Success: Diagnosing Failures in Long-Horizon Security LLM Agents
items.abstract: Long-horizon security LLM agents must carry information and decisions across many dependent interactions, where later actions often depend on services, state, or access discovered much earlier. This makes final task success difficult to interpret: an agent may fail before it ever reaches the point where the capability of interest can be exercised. We present a diagnostic methodology that instruments security tasks with checkpoints, separates failures before and after capability exposure, and uses controlled interventions to test suspected upstream bottlenecks. We evaluate the methodology across four task families involving delayed reuse of discovered information, reuse of observed state, recovery from failed strategies, and decision making after uncertain outcomes. On observed state reuse, checkpoint analysis shows that many Gemini 2.5 Flash failures occur before the model observes the state it is later expected to reuse. In a pre-specified 92-seed study, targeted protocol-disambiguation guidance increases state observation from 65.5\% under a matched non-guidance control message to 95.4\%. Repeating the same design with Gemini 3.7 Flash produces the opposite effect, while state ob

_analysis.summary: This paper studies why advanced AI agents designed for security tasks often fail in complex, multi-step scenarios. It introduces a diagnostic method to pinpoint where these failures occur—whether early in the process (e.g., accessing tools or data) or later when the agent tries to use a capability it never properly obtained. The findings highlight how upstream bottlenecks (like access restrictions or tool discovery) can cascade into final failures, even if the agent’s core abilities are sound.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how AI agents’ dependency on upstream access (e.g., APIs, data, or tools) can create structural barriers to entry or expansion for smaller firms, reinforcing dominance by gatekeepers who control these resources.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents’ reliance on upstream access points (e.g., APIs, cloud services) signals a shift toward platform-controlled ecosystems, where gatekeepers can leverage access restrictions to maintain market power.

items.title: Monotone Allocations without Single-Crossing: When to Bunch and When to Jump
items.abstract: A principal screens an agent whose technology has a minimum efficient scale, so the Spence-Mirrlees condition fails along a monotone dividing curve: the locus at which every type values marginal output equally. For the class in which this curve and the relaxed solution are both strictly monotone, the optimal contract obeys a trichotomy, governed by how the two meet: a jump is impossible when they never meet, unavoidable across a flat dividing curve, a choice across a strictly increasing one. The optimum is found, not conjectured: each solution is certified as globally optimal among all implementable allocations, deterministic or random, by dualizing the family of binding constraints through an explicit weight; the certificates require neither linear primitives nor any restriction on the shape of the contract. Under mild regularity the class comprises exactly forty configurations; each is mapped to its forced shape, solved in closed form, and certified.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how a principal (e.g., a regulator or platform) designs optimal contracts for an agent (e.g., a firm or user) when the agent's technology has a minimum efficient scale, causing the Spence-Mirrlees condition—a key assumption in screening models—to fail. The study finds that the optimal contract follows one of three outcomes (a 'trichotomy') depending on how a monotone dividing curve (where marginal output is valued equally by all types) interacts with the relaxed solution: no meeting (no jump), a flat curve (unavoidable jump), or a strictly increasing curve (choice).
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on principal-agent theory, its insights into how minimum efficient scales and monotone dividing curves shape optimal contracts could indirectly inform discussions on platform regulation and market design in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals the importance of understanding non-linear cost structures and threshold effects in digital platforms, which may influence how regulators assess market power and pricing behavior.

items.title: Conformity Traps and the Formation of Independent Judgment
items.abstract: I study why some groups---polities and organizations alike---sustain independent judgment while others fall into conformity traps. Social approval can suppress not only the expression of independent judgment but also the upstream practice that keeps such judgment available: maintaining judgment generates visible questioning, and observers cannot distinguish diligence from opposition. Because suspicion falls when questioning is common, the same desire for approval can sustain a questioning culture or a conformity trap. The model separates maintaining judgment from acting on it when novelty arrives. When the decision to act is uniquely determined, I give primitive conditions for coexistence; in a logit--proportional benchmark, a single inequality is necessary and sufficient. The principal contribution is dynamic. Under staggered revision the stock of judgment is inherited: protecting dissent releases existing judgment at once---with negative expected adaptive value on impact in a stationary culture below a break-even competence threshold---whereas rebuilding the stock is constrained by turnover. A monotone operator constructs the extremal perfect-foresight paths from every inherited

_analysis.summary: This paper examines why some groups (like companies or societies) encourage independent thinking while others suppress it through conformity. It argues that the desire for social approval can either sustain a culture of questioning or lead to a 'conformity trap' where people avoid challenging norms to avoid suspicion. The model distinguishes between *maintaining judgment* (the practice of keeping critical thinking alive) and *acting on it* (applying judgment when new information arises).
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Relevant for digital competition policy because it explains how conformity pressures in tech platforms (e.g., avoiding dissent to maintain approval) can stifle innovation and competition, particularly in algorithmic decision-making environments.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals that conformity pressures in tech ecosystems may reduce competitive pressure by discouraging disruptive innovation or critique of dominant platforms.

items.title: Characterizing the Plurality Rule via Clone Invariance
items.abstract: The Plurality rule is vulnerable to vote splitting between similar alternatives. Defying conventional wisdom, we characterize the Plurality rule through a specific type of clone independence condition. We further introduce the notion of a one-parameter family of $p$-Clone Resistance ($p$-CR), and examine the property within the class of scoring rules. For $p \in (0,1)$, nontrivial rules exist with at most three alternatives, but only the Trivial rule generally satisfies the condition.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines the Plurality rule (a voting system where the candidate with the most votes wins) and finds it is vulnerable to 'vote splitting' when similar alternatives exist. It introduces a new concept called 'p-Clone Resistance' to analyze how voting rules handle similar options, showing that only trivial rules fully satisfy this condition beyond three alternatives.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on voting systems, its insights into how 'clone' alternatives (similar options) can distort outcomes may indirectly inform discussions on platform self-preferencing or algorithmic ranking in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that algorithmic systems (even in non-digital contexts) must account for 'clone' effects, which could translate to concerns about how platforms manipulate rankings or suppress competitive alternatives.

items.title: Coalitional Manipulation of Set-Valued Median Voting
items.abstract: We study coalitional manipulation of interval-valued median correspondences on the single-peaked domain. Under the pessimistic extension, group strategy-proofness rules out any genuinely set-valued choice. Under the optimistic and best--worst extensions, by contrast, group strategy-proofness characterizes target set correspondences. Moreover, coalitions of at most two voters suffice for both the impossibility and characterization results. Thus, coalitional robustness sharply restricts, but need not eliminate, set-valued flexibility.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how small groups of voters (coalitions of just two) can manipulate voting systems that use interval-valued median rules to make decisions. It finds that under certain interpretations of these rules, such manipulation is impossible, while under others, it reveals that flexible set-based choices can still be robust to manipulation. The study uses concepts like 'group strategy-proofness' (a voting system where no coalition can manipulate outcomes) and 'set-valued choice' (where outcomes are ranges rather than single options).
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on voting theory, its insights into coalition-based manipulation and robustness of set-valued systems could inform discussions on algorithmic decision-making in digital platforms, particularly where user preferences or rankings are aggregated.
