_analysis.market_signal: This signals the importance of studying coalition dynamics in algorithmic systems, which may become relevant for assessing market power in recommendation systems or ranking algorithms used by digital platforms.

items.title: Europe's Climate Ambition Under Scrutiny: Evidence from Deep Learning Emission Projections
items.abstract: The European Union has committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions 55% below 1990 levels by 2030, but whether current trends are compatible with this ambition remains uncertain. We apply deep learning to high-resolution socioeconomic and sectoral data across EU27 member states till 2023 to project sectoral CO$_2$ trajectories under current trends, extrapolating observed sectoral momentum without assuming changes in the pace or effectiveness of the policy environment beyond what is already reflected in historical data. We project that EU27 emissions will exceed the 2030 target by 35% (620 Mt CO$_2$ shortfall), with only a small minority of countries on trajectories consistent with the bloc's commitments. While the Power sector achieves target-consistent reductions driven by the renewable transition, Mobility shows minimal progress and accounts for over a third of total emissions by 2030, reflecting a structural inertia across member states rather than geographically concentrated lag. Our findings indicate that substantial additional intervention is required to close Europe's ambition-implementation gap, and call for establishing up-to-date energy information in Europe.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper uses deep learning (a type of AI that learns from large datasets) to predict future CO2 emissions across the EU. It finds that, based on current trends, the EU is unlikely to meet its 2030 climate target, with emissions projected to exceed the goal by 35% (620 million metric tons). The study does not assume any future policy changes beyond what is already reflected in historical data.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on climate policy, its use of deep learning to model sectoral trends could indirectly inform discussions on AI's role in digital markets and data-driven competition.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals the growing importance of AI-driven modeling in policy and industry forecasting, which may influence how regulators assess data access and market power in digital sectors.

items.title: Accounting for intra-household joint travel in agent-based transport simulations
items.abstract: Intra-household joint home-based tours - trips in which household members depart together, engage in shared activities, and return together - represent a significant share of daily travel, yet are systematically ignored in transport simulations. Conflating joint and solo tours within a single mode choice framework introduces bias in preference parameter estimates. This paper proposes a three-step methodology to integrate joint tours in agent-based transport models: a Random Forest classifier to identify joint tours, a Multinomial Logit model estimating mode choice specific to joint tours, and a Penalized Logistic Regression for driver/passenger assignment. Applied to the Paris region using household travel survey data, the methodology successfully replicates observed joint tour shares and mode distributions in a synthetic population. The proposed framework enables more reliable evaluation of policies whose impacts differ between joint and solo travel, such as HOV lanes or family transit fare discounts.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper highlights a gap in transport simulation models by showing that joint household trips (where family members travel together) are often overlooked, leading to biased estimates of travel preferences. It proposes a three-step method—using a Random Forest classifier and a Multinomial Logit model—to better account for these shared journeys in agent-based transport simulations.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on transport modeling, its methodology for distinguishing joint vs. solo activities could inform data-driven approaches in digital markets, such as analyzing joint user behavior in platform ecosystems.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals the growing importance of granular, agent-based modeling in understanding complex user interactions, which may influence how digital platforms assess user behavior and market dynamics.

items.title: CentaurBench: Benchmarking LLM Capabilities on Augmenting vs. Automating Real-World Work Tasks
items.abstract: Most LLM benchmarks rank models on their ability to automate work tasks. In practice, however, models are often used to assist other (human or LLM) agents. The question that drives model selection is therefore not only which model produces the best output, but which model most improves the work of another (weaker) agent. We introduce a unified framework that evaluates the capability of models to automate and augment another agent's performance. Across seven economically grounded real-world tasks, an assistant model writes assistance text for a standardized lower-capacity worker model, which produces the deliverable. In automation mode, the assistant produces the output directly. Outputs are scored through blind pairwise comparisons by an LLM judge panel with task-specific rubrics, replicated across ten runs. Rankings across the two regimes are only modestly correlated, and the automation winner loses augmentation on five of seven tasks. Assistance is not reliably positive. The unaided worker outranks every assisted condition on three tasks, and only one model's guidance beats no guidance on average. These results suggest that automation ability is an incomplete proxy for assistance

_analysis.summary: This academic paper introduces a new benchmark called CentaurBench, which evaluates large language models (LLMs) not just on their ability to fully automate tasks, but on their ability to *augment* the work of other agents (human or AI). The study finds that the best model for automation isn’t always the best for assistance, highlighting how model selection in real-world applications depends on collaborative performance rather than standalone capability.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work signals a shift in how AI models are valued in digital markets—from standalone performance to collaborative augmentation—potentially reshaping demand for AI tools and the competitive dynamics between AI providers.
_analysis.market_signal: AI models that excel at augmenting human or AI workers may gain a competitive edge over those optimized solely for automation, altering market incentives and adoption patterns.

items.title: Stable Matching with Peer-Dependent Preferences: Existence and Cutoff Characterization
items.abstract: This paper presents a framework for stable matching markets that accommodates the peer-dependent preferences employed in empirical work. We show the existence of a stable matching in a continuum economy and of an approximately stable matching in a large finite sampled economy under assumptions satisfied by standard empirical specifications. The analysis builds on a tractable characterization of stable matchings with peer-dependent preferences in terms of supply and demand equations along with a rational-expectations condition.

_analysis.summary: This paper develops a mathematical framework for stable matching markets where preferences depend on peers (e.g., how one person's choices affect another's). It proves that stable matchings exist in large economies and provides a way to approximate them in real-world settings using supply and demand equations. The work builds on rational-expectations assumptions common in empirical models.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper advances matching theory, it does not directly address digital competition policy but offers tools that could model platform-mediated interactions (e.g., gig economy labor markets).
_analysis.market_signal: Signals growing academic interest in peer-dependent dynamics, which may later inform platform regulation or antitrust analysis of two-sided markets.

items.title: The Fragility of Social Learning with Noisy Messages
items.abstract: We examine how agents learn when information from original sources only reaches them after noisy relay. A receiver learns if and only if they have access to sufficiently many chains of noisy relay and they perfectly understand the noise process. However, even slight uncertainty over message mutation rates makes learning from long chains impossible, no matter how many independent sources are accessed.

_analysis.summary: This paper studies how people learn when information gets distorted as it spreads through multiple sources. It finds that people can only learn correctly if they get many independent versions of the same message and fully understand how the noise (distortion) works. Even small doubts about how much the message changes make learning from long chains of information impossible.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Highlights how information distortion in digital ecosystems (e.g., social media, recommendation systems) can undermine accurate decision-making, which is critical for assessing consumer harm and market power in digital platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals that information intermediaries (like social media or AI-driven content platforms) may inadvertently or deliberately amplify noise, complicating consumer protection and competition enforcement.

items.title: How AI Prompts Can Teach Us About the Structure of Human Behavior
items.abstract: We introduce a general, easy-to-implement AI-based method for studying the structure and complexity of human behavior. We assign a large language model a ``type vector'' and then prompt it to choose actions across settings in which we observe human choices. For instance, the type vector (2,4) becomes ``You are a player characterized by the following profile: 2 out of 5 in Altruism, 4 out of 5 in Risk Aversion,'' after which it is prompted to make choices. We vary the dimensions (e.g., Altruism, Fairness, Trust, $\dots$) and values (e.g., 1--5) to minimize distance to human choices. Applying the method to 119,147 decisions made by 78,657 subjects from more than 35 countries across 10 classic economic game roles, we find that human behavior can be closely matched using three dimensions: Risk Aversion, Strategic Sophistication, and Trust. Moreover, the types needed to fit individuals across games cluster into fewer than a dozen groups, and can predict behavior in held-out games with different rules and available actions. The results suggest that behavior across diverse settings can be approximated by a low-dimensional, portable representation, supporting the possibility of general yet

_analysis.summary: This paper presents a method using large language models (LLMs) to simulate human behavior by assigning 'type vectors' (e.g., levels of altruism or risk aversion) and prompting the AI to make choices. The goal is to minimize the distance between AI-generated choices and observed human behavior, offering insights into the structure of human decision-making.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on behavioral modeling rather than competition policy, its method for simulating human-like decision-making could inform studies of algorithmic behavior in digital markets or consumer interactions with AI systems.
_analysis.market_signal: The use of LLMs to model human behavior signals growing sophistication in AI-driven decision-making tools that may influence digital market dynamics, particularly in consumer-facing platforms.

items.title: Revisiting the Intra-Team Communication Method to Elicit Level-k Reasoning in Beauty Contests and 11-20 Games
items.abstract: How level-0 players behave and how they are perceived by higher-level players are central questions in the literature on level-k models of boundedly rational strategic reasoning. To study these twin questions, we apply the intra-team communication method developed by Burchardi and Penczynski (2014) to identify level-0 actions and beliefs in the canonical beauty contest game and in a variant of the 11-20 game of Goeree et al. (2018), in which behavior appears inconsistent with the standard level-k model. In the beauty contest game, we replicate Burchardi and Penczynski (2014)'s finding that elicited level-0 beliefs align with observed level-0 actions. In the variant of the 11-20 game, however, elicited level-0 beliefs and observed level-0 actions diverge, and both depart from the standard level-0 assumption, suggesting a complementary explanation for the behavioral pattern documented by Goeree et al. (2018).

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how people with limited strategic reasoning (called 'level-0 players') behave and are perceived in games like the beauty contest and the 11-20 game, using a method where players communicate within teams. It finds that higher-level players (those with more sophisticated reasoning) adjust their strategies based on how they expect level-0 players to act, revealing insights into bounded rationality in competitive settings.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on behavioral economics and strategic reasoning, its findings on how players perceive and adapt to less sophisticated actors could indirectly inform models of competitive dynamics in digital markets where firms or AI systems interact with less sophisticated participants.
_analysis.market_signal: The study signals that understanding bounded rationality and communication within teams may become more relevant as AI systems increasingly interact with human or algorithmic agents in digital markets.

items.title: Does the grand coalition form? Persistence, arrival, and the role of the sharing rule in a dynamic process of nested binding agreements
items.abstract: We study a dynamic coalition-formation process in the tradition of Konishi and Ray (2003): players repeatedly form and dissolve binding agreements, evaluate states by discounted long-term expected payoffs, and hold self-confirming beliefs about the process. States and payoff sharing follow Heitzig and Kornek (2018): a state is a hierarchy of nested agreements; agreements are formed by merging existing top-level coalitions, and are terminated together with all agreements containing them; and the members of a new agreement share the surplus it generates, measured against the state without that agreement. All payoff assumptions are structural. We prove that every grand state ever reached is absorbing, and that every absorbing state is grand, for every discount factor. A grand state is actually reached, almost surely, in three cases: small discount factors; three players; and, for any number of players and all discount factors, whenever every player prefers every grand state to every non-grand state in static payoffs, as when distributional stakes are smaller than each player's share of the efficiency gain. Otherwise the process can fail only by cycling for ever among non-grand states.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how groups form and dissolve binding agreements over time, using a model where players merge existing coalitions and share the resulting benefits. It explores how these coalitions persist or change based on long-term payoffs and shared rules.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on coalition formation in general, its insights into hierarchical agreements and surplus sharing could apply to digital platform ecosystems, though it does not explicitly address competition or antitrust.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals potential dynamics in digital market structures where platforms or firms form nested partnerships or alliances.

items.title: Governing Delegation to Generative Artificial Intelligence: Human Direction, Work-Related Orientation, and Modes of Use
items.abstract: Delegating cognitive operations to generative artificial intelligence redistributes execution and raises a governance problem: where human direction of the task remains. We distinguish two routes. Specified delegation places that direction before execution, through instructions, constraints, or criteria that delimit the task. Iterative coproduction places it during production, through interventions that correct or redirect provisional outputs. To examine both routes, we use aggregate monthly cells from the Anthropic Economic Index for April and May 2026. The AEI distinguishes two modes of use: 1P API, which corresponds to direct traffic through Anthropic's API, and Claude.ai, which combines activity from Chat and Cowork. On this basis, we test whether a stronger work-related orientation of human-AI interaction is associated with more specified delegation within each mode and whether the increase in the iterative profile is greater in Claude.ai than in 1P API. The main analysis uses level-0 O*NET tasks and estimates how both profiles change when an eligible record reallocates ten percentage points from personal use to work-related use. The iterative comparison is restricted to 1,411

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how humans delegate tasks to generative AI (AI systems that create content like text or images) and the governance challenges that arise. It identifies two main ways humans guide AI: 'specified delegation' (giving clear instructions upfront) and 'iterative coproduction' (correcting AI outputs as they are being created). The study uses data from the Anthropic Economic Index (AEI) to analyze these methods.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper highlights how AI delegation models could reshape labor markets and firm boundaries, indirectly influencing digital competition by altering how firms integrate AI tools.
_analysis.market_signal: AI delegation models may accelerate the shift toward AI-augmented work, potentially disrupting traditional digital labor markets and firm hierarchies.

items.title: Searchable Menus
items.abstract: Multidimensional screening is (in)famously intractable. In this paper, we study optimal screening mechanisms subject to a tractability constraint from the agent's perspective. Specifically, we require that the menu of options offered by the designer can be ordered so that, regardless of her preference type, the agent can find a utility-maximizing option via greedy search: any locally optimal choice must also be globally optimal. In one-dimensional screening with the single-crossing property, this requirement has no bite. In multidimensional environments, however, searchability restricts the set of implementable outcomes. In the multiproduct monopoly problem, the optimal searchable menu is a sparse upgrade menu: higher tiers offer higher allocation probabilities for every good, and the number of tiers is at most the number of goods. In a multidimensional screening problem with money and ordeals, the optimal searchable menu offers the agent a single way to obtain the good. In income taxation with rich multidimensional heterogeneity, a tax schedule is searchable if and only if it is progressive.

_analysis.summary: This paper studies how to design optimal menus of choices (like pricing tiers or product options) when dealing with complex, multidimensional problems. It introduces a 'searchability' constraint, requiring that users can find the best option by simply picking the locally best choice at each step, which is easier than solving the full problem. In simple cases, this doesn't change much, but in complex markets (like digital platforms), it restricts the designer's options significantly.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The paper's focus on designing 'searchable' menus in multidimensional environments could inform how digital platforms structure their offerings to avoid antitrust concerns, such as self-preferencing or unfair trading conditions.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that digital platforms may need to simplify their product menus or interfaces to comply with competition rules, potentially reducing complexity-driven market power.

items.title: The Long-Term Effects of British and French Colonization in Africa on Trust in Traditional Leaders
items.abstract: Trust in local institutions matters for trade, public goods provision, conflict resolution, and democratic consolidation. Using individual data from rounds 6 and 7 of the Afrobarometer surveys, I document that respondents in former British colonies are substantially more likely to trust traditional leaders than respondents in former French colonies. Cross-country comparisons of this kind are confounded by unobserved heterogeneity in pre- and post-colonial histories. To make progress on identification, I focus on Cameroon, which contains regions colonized by Britain and regions colonized by France within a single modern state, and I exploit the former colonial partition line as a geographic discontinuity, comparing respondents who live close to either side of the anglophone-francophone boundary. The theoretical argument is that the two colonial powers differed systematically in how they treated customary authority: British indirect rule preserved the governance functions of chiefs, while French direct rule subordinated chiefs to the administration and assigned them its most coercive tasks, taxation and forced labor above all, and these divergent experiences shaped the legitimacy of

_analysis.summary: This study examines how historical colonial institutions in Africa influence trust in traditional leaders today. Using survey data from Cameroon, which has regions colonized by both Britain and France, it finds that people in former British colonies are significantly more likely to trust traditional leaders than those in former French colonies. The research uses Cameroon as a case study to control for other historical differences between countries.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the study focuses on historical institutional trust rather than digital markets, its methodological approach to isolating causal effects in comparative settings could inform competition policy research on platform governance or trust in digital institutions.
_analysis.market_signal: This paper signals the importance of historical institutional design in shaping contemporary governance structures, which may have indirect implications for digital platform regulation and trust in algorithmic systems.

items.title: Conservation of Short-term Flows: Signed Optimal Transport
items.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework for signed optimal transport. A global flatness measure induced by the continuum transport equation serves as the regularizer. We examine transport networks from a harmonic analysis perspective, prove the existence and uniqueness of the optimal coupling in the variational problem, and provide an algorithmic scheme that guarantees lossless information transport under bi-marginal constraints. To bridge theory with practice, we design an empirical analysis framework for the resulting optimal estimators, which is sufficiently general to accommodate both time-series and panel-structural analyses of the network, owing to the intrinsic invariance properties of locally compact abelian groups.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces a new mathematical framework called *signed optimal transport* to model how information or resources move efficiently between systems while preserving key properties. It proves mathematically that such transfers can be lossless and provides algorithms to implement this in practice, with applications in data analysis and network optimization.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While mathematically innovative, the paper does not directly address digital competition policy, market power, or antitrust concerns.
_analysis.market_signal: This research signals potential advancements in data-efficient algorithms that could influence how platforms optimize resource allocation, but it does not yet indicate a market disruption.

items.title: Reputation and institutional certification as complementary trust mechanisms in a single online market
items.abstract: Reputation and institutional certification are the two main trust mechanisms under information asymmetry, yet their interaction remains poorly understood. We analyze nearly one million fixed-price eBay listings of Pokemon cards, where sellers choose among three signals: third-party grading (institutional certification), self-grading (a self-claimed condition description), or no signal. We show that self-grading and third-party grading dominate distinct regions of the reputation-value space, with the self-grading region widening as reputation rises. Reputation also amplifies the price premium of self-grading but not that of third-party grading. We develop a signaling game in which a false self-claim carries an ex-post cost proportional to reputation, whereas certification carries an ex-ante cost independent of reputation. These costs split the reputation-value space into equilibrium regimes that explain both patterns. The two mechanisms are therefore substitutes within a transaction yet complements across the market, replacing the reputation-versus-institution dichotomy with a regime structure set by reputation and value.

_analysis.summary: This study examines how two trust-building mechanisms—reputation systems (like seller ratings) and third-party certification (such as professional grading)—affect pricing and competition in online markets. Using data from nearly one million eBay listings for Pokémon cards, the authors find that sellers with strong reputations rely more on self-grading (their own condition descriptions), while third-party grading is preferred by less-established sellers. As sellers build better reputations, the advantage of self-grading grows, suggesting these mechanisms serve different roles in reducing buyer uncertainty.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how trust mechanisms shape market dynamics in digital platforms, which is relevant for understanding how platform policies (e.g., rating systems) influence competition and consumer behavior.
_analysis.market_signal: Shows how alternative trust signals (like third-party certification) can coexist with or complement reputation systems in digital markets, potentially reducing barriers to entry for smaller sellers.

items.title: Bayesian Signaling and Entry Decisions under Uncertain Market Conditions
items.abstract: We develop a continuous-time entry-deterrence game in which market demand evolves according to the Chan-Karolyi-Longstaff-Sanders (CKLS) stochastic differential equation, allowing mean reversion and state-dependent volatility. An incumbent with privately known strength strategically chooses advertising and promotional expenditures to influence a potential entrant's beliefs, while the entrant faces a costly, irreversible entry decision and optimally waits until market conditions justify participation. Within a dynamic Stackelberg setting, Bayesian learning, asymmetric information, stochastic demand, and strategic controls jointly determine entry and signaling behavior. Using a Feynman-type path-integral control formulation, we characterize a Markovian Nash feedback equilibrium for the firms' expenditure strategies. Our contribution is to integrate CKLS demand uncertainty, private information, irreversible entry, Bayesian belief updating, and path-integral feedback control within a unified continuous-time entry-deterrence framework, while providing a computational alternative to direct Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) approach. We illustrate the framework empirically using 2010-2024 rev

_analysis.summary: This paper models how an established company (the 'incumbent') can use advertising and promotions to signal its strength to a potential rival, deterring market entry under uncertain demand conditions. The model uses a mathematical framework to show how the incumbent’s private information and the entrant’s costly, irreversible decision interact in a dynamic game where market demand fluctuates unpredictably.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Provides theoretical insights into how incumbents in digital markets may use strategic signaling (e.g., advertising) to deter entry, relevant for understanding platform dominance and barriers to competition.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals that incumbents in digital markets may rely on costly signaling (like ads) to maintain dominance, reinforcing barriers to entry for rivals.

items.title: Fictitious credit limits, real fees. President of UOKiK brings charges against the Supergrosz platform

_analysis.summary: Poland’s competition authority (UOKiK) has accused the Supergrosz platform of misleading consumers by advertising fictitious credit limits while charging high fees. synthesis.headline: AI agents poised to fragment digital markets, warns new research wave
synthesis.executive_summary: A surge of academic work in August 2026 suggests AI agents and large language models (LLMs) are reshaping digital markets by enabling new entrants to compete with incumbents like Google and Amazon. Regulators are still catching up: the EU’s DMA (Digital Markets Act) remains the main active tool, while courts have not yet issued binding rulings on AI-driven market power. Meanwhile, academic papers predict that AI agents will fragment ecosystems, erode winner-takes-all dynamics, and challenge platform gatekeepers. One study shows Netflix’s recommender system already shifts consumption from ‘superstars’ to the ‘middle-tail’ [#1], while another warns that opaque algorithmic commitment could distort competition [#3]. These findings matter because they signal where enforcement may focus next—especially around interoperability, data access, and algorithmic transparency.

Another study shows AI-driven catalog enrichment tools could help smaller e-commerce players compete with Amazon by improving product data [#53]. These findings suggest AI agents may fragment digital markets, eroding the dominance of incumbents.

faq.question: What does interoperability mean?
faq.answer: Interoperability means different systems or tools can work together seamlessly, like a USB drive that plugs into any computer. In AI, it means AI agents (e.g., Amazon Kiro and Google Gemini) can share outputs or collaborate without proprietary barriers. For users, it means switching between services (e.g., email providers) without losing functionality or data.
